notes.meaning: Work on the temple had been stopped for about fifteen years, and the people had grown comfortable leaving God's house in ruins. God raised up the prophets Haggai and Zechariah to speak directly to the Jews in Judah and Jerusalem. They spoke with God's authority, urging the people to turn away from their excuses and get back to work.

Zerubbabel the governor and Jeshua the high priest responded right away to the prophets' preaching and restarted the building. Haggai and Zechariah did not simply give speeches; they stood with the leaders and helped them with the work. God used the bold preaching of His word to stir up the leaders with fresh courage.

Tattenai, the Persian governor over the whole region west of the Euphrates River, arrived in Jerusalem with his officials to investigate. They questioned the Jews, asking who gave them permission to rebuild the temple and its walls. Unlike earlier hostile neighbors, Tattenai came as a careful ruler checking whether this project was lawful.

The Persian officials also asked for the names of the men leading the construction. They wanted a written list so they could hold those specific leaders responsible if the king found anything unlawful. The Jewish builders answered openly because they had nothing to hide and were not ashamed of their work.

God watched over the Jewish elders with His special care and protection. Because the Lord was guarding them, Tattenai did not force them to stop working while he wrote to King Darius. The builders were allowed to keep making progress for months while waiting for the royal reply to return.

Tattenai and his fellow officials sent a formal letter to King Darius of Persia. The letter opened with a respectful greeting, wishing the king total peace. It was an official report meant to give the king an honest, calm summary of what was happening in Jerusalem.

The officials reported to the king that they had visited Judah and inspected the temple of the great God. They noted that the builders were using huge stones and placing strong wooden beams into the walls. They stated fairly that the work was moving quickly and succeeding under the Jews' hands.

Tattenai explained to the king how he had questioned the Jewish elders about who authorized the building. He also told Darius that he asked for the leaders' names so the king would know exactly who was in charge. The governor reported these facts accurately without making up false accusations.

The elders gave a clear confession of their faith, calling themselves servants of the God of heaven and earth. They explained that they were not starting a new movement, but rebuilding a temple that had stood for centuries. That original house of God had been completed long ago by Solomon, a great king of Israel.

The elders did not hide their nation's past shame, but openly admitted that their ancestors had provoked God to anger. They explained that Babylon had not conquered them by superior might, but because God gave them over to King Nebuchadnezzar as punishment. Nebuchadnezzar then destroyed their temple and carried the people into exile.

The elders showed that their legal authority came from King Cyrus in his very first year of ruling Babylon. Cyrus had issued an official royal decree granting the Jews permission to return and rebuild the temple. This proved they were acting in obedience to Persian law rather than starting a rebellion.

Cyrus had also returned the sacred gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had stolen from Jerusalem. The king placed these treasures into the care of a governor named Sheshbazzar and sent him to carry them home. Cyrus commanded that these articles be put back and that the temple be rebuilt on its original holy ground.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern commentators view Sheshbazzar as a distinct Persian-appointed official who led the first return, rather than another name for Zerubbabel.

notes.meaning: Sheshbazzar arrived in Jerusalem years earlier and laid the foundation of God's house. The elders explained that the building project had been underway ever since, though many hindrances had kept it from being finished. They were showing the governor that their current work was simply finishing what the Persian crown had already approved.

Tattenai closed his letter by asking King Darius to search the royal archives in Babylon to confirm Cyrus's decree. He did not ask the king to stop the work or punish anyone, but asked for the king's official ruling based on the facts. God used this fair-minded request to protect His people and verify their right to finish the temple.
